subtopic: PRECEDENCE OP GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAY, MARCH 27, AND WEDNESDAY, MARCH 29
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, March 23, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave notice that today he would move the following motion:
That on Monday, the 27th of March instant, and on Wednesday, the 29th of March instant, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all business except the introduction of bills, questions and. notices of motions for the production of papers.
On Friday night I announced that this motion would be moved today. In the absence of the Prime Minister, on his behalf I now move the motion.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: IDENTIFICATION FORMS REQUIRED AT BORDER POINTS ON LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Revenue with regard to an order made by his department, to become effective next Thursday, under which the making out of new automobile identification forms is required to be made daily at the port of exit, or on every occasion on which a Canadian motorist crosses the border to visit the United States. This regulation, if carried out at such places as Windsor, Ontario; North Portal, Saskatchewan; White Rock, British Columbia, and other places-

subtopic: IDENTIFICATION FORMS REQUIRED AT BORDER POINTS ON LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: Don't forget Niagara Falls.

subtopic: IDENTIFICATION FORMS REQUIRED AT BORDER POINTS ON LEAVING CANADA
speechtext:
I did mention that there were other places, and I should have mentioned Niagara Falls and Prescott. This order will discourage traffic and result in chaos. It would seem to be a needless requirement. Will the minister reconsider the matter, and,


instead of enforcing this order requiring the form to be signed each day, follow the old system of having one form operative for a year?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: IDENTIFICATION FORMS REQUIRED AT BORDER POINTS ON LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: It is not a matter of giving reconsideration to an order that, has gone out. There has been a very slight change in our system in order to ensure better control of Canadian automobile traffic to the United States. We are continuing the system heretofore in effect for border residents who have occasion to go to the United States regularly. The change does not in any way affect our American tourists coming to Canada.

subtopic: IDENTIFICATION FORMS REQUIRED AT BORDER POINTS ON LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: Perhaps I might ask a question arising out of the minister's answer. Is there not a new regulation which requires that a form be signed each time a person enters the United States? That is the information the officials at border points have. Will the minister explain what the new regulation is? He says that it does not affect certain points, but does it apply to all other ports of entry?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: IDENTIFICATION FORMS REQUIRED AT BORDER POINTS ON LEAVING CANADA
speechtext: The new order will not affect people at border points who are in the habit of crossing regularly. They will have permits to indicate that they cross regularly, and those permits will be honoured for a period of six months. Persons who do not cross regularly will be required to fill in the form now being issued. There will be no inconvenience to those who live in Canada and go to the United States regularly and are known to the officers at the different ports of exit.

Mr. Speaker, before this bill is given second reading there are certain matters which I think should be discussed to a greater extent than was the case when the resolution which foreshadowed this bill was before the house. The house will remember that we gave consent to the resolution passing and to having the discussion on the resolution which preceded Bill No. 17, to amend the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
We contend that the principle involved in this bill, that of setting up a board in Canada to take care of the export of surplus agricultural products, should be placed on a permanent basis rather than be extended from year to year as in the past, depending on the state of emergency which exists as a result of the war. We have followed that procedure for the last four years, and as a result of the temporary methods which have been followed we have

Agricultural Products Act lost most of our markets for surplus agricultural products. So far as we are concerned we see no possible way of winning back those markets under this type of legislation. Only when we have permanent legislation shall we be able to make agreements and supply our customers, not only in England but in European countries, with products which are uniform, and which we can guarantee to supply regularly from year to year. The European market is demanding uniformity of quality in the products supplied to them, and continuity of supply. I do not think that is possible unless there is permanent legislation to provide for the supplying of those markets.
Surpluses of agricultural products are beginning to appear all over the North American continent. The international federation of agricultural producers, when they met in Paris in 1948, realized this problem. They stated in their report:
It is essential that effective machinery should be provided to deal with any surpluses that may develop, to ensure that they are directed to areas of the greatest need, and that such surpluses should not be allowed to undermine the world price structure.
When this organization met at Guelph, *Ontario, a year ago, they came to the same conclusion, and they set up a committee which would make recommendations to the food and agricultural organization at their meeting in Washington last year. That committee recommended at Washington that an organization should be set up under FAO for the distribution of surplus agricultural products to needy areas throughout the world. The recommendation of IFAP was not accepted by the food and agricultural organization, which set up a commodity committee to endeavour to ascertain the best way to distribute surplus products. If we are to work in conjunction with international organizations, we must have a national export act under which surpluses can be collected in Canada and turned over, when the time comes, to the international organization for distribution in the needy areas of the world.
As a matter of fact the Minister of Agriculture, addressing the food and agricultural organization in Washington, indicated it was his opinion that the national government should set up some organization for performing this particular function.
He said:
Any transactions developed under the short term trading functions will be subject to concurrence by the governments concerned, and the major details of such transactions will also be subject to agreement by governments.
This being the case it hardly seems necessary to have an international agency actually buying and selling in commodity markets. It may even be questioned whether such activity in commodity markets by an international agency is desirable. It

seems to us, therefore, that the question of the creation of a large capital fund for such a purpose is not necessarily an issue.
Later he stated:
Lord Boyd Orr, in presenting his proposal for a world food board, had in mind the fact that the world had surpluses during certain periods and extreme shortages in other periods. It was his purpose to stabilize returns to producers and costs to consumers by setting aside surplus quantities in good years for periods of shortages. As has been pointed out in other conferences, however, national governments can, and do, perform this function . . .
In other words, it is one of the functions under the present measure which we are extending for one year, but we are only renewing it for one year and we do not believe that is sufficient. The minister went on to say:
Canada, for example, has provided for the holding of stocks of wheat under government control. Moreover, it is probably consistent with other developments to envision the long-term holding of stocks as an element in an over-all commodity agreement.
I agree with the minister. If we are to carry out what he stated as government policy before the food and agricultural organization, we must have something more permanent than the act which we are now extending for one year. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce):
That Bill No. 16 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introducing of a permanent agricultural products export act which would provide for the setting up of an export board, to fill present contracts, negotiate future contracts, and develop new markets abroad for surplus agricultural products.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure many of my constituents would wish me to say a few words on this subject, particularly in view of the remarks that have been made by members of the various opposition parties. No one will deny the importance of the British market so far as agricultural products are concerned, and this is particularly true with respect to wheat. It becomes important indeed when

we recall that to a certain extent almost the entire economy of the west is directly or indirectly controlled1 by the price of wheat.
In the discussion it has become apparent that our C.C.F. friends place squarely upon the shoulders of the government the blame for our loss of export trade, particularly the reduction of our agricultural exports to the United Kingdom. They would like us to believe that if there have been reductions in the sale of certain agricultural products, that lessening in export trade is due entirely to the policies or attitude of this administration. Of course we know that many factors were entirely beyond the control of this government. In order to remedy this situation, our C.C.F. friends in this house have suggested ways and means of recapturing these markets; or, as the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) put it, if certain things had been done these markets would not have been lost during the past few years. In order that I may be accurate in my reference to his remarks, I should like to quote from page 1059 of Hansard of the present session. After referring to the lack of dollars in Great Britain with which to buy our agricultural products, he said:
. . . under which we would have accepted British goods in exchange for our food, we would have been able to make agreements similar to those which Britain has made with many other countries.
That is a very easy solution, Mr. Speaker. In other words the hon. member says that if the British people have not dollars with which to buy our products, all we have to do is trade produce for produce. Naturally if there is a shortage of dollars in Great Britain it is due to the fact the people were not able to exchange products on a basis that would enable them to secure dollars. The problem, therefore, is still in front of us. This suggestion is not a solution of that problem.
The leader of the C.C.F. party went one step further with the same argument, and suggested that if the British people have not the necessary dollars to purchase our agricultural products, then we should accept sterling; trade could be resumed on that basis. Again this is no solution to the problem. It is a similar attempt to the one just mentioned, because, after all, to accept sterling is merely to sell on credit. Putting it on an individual basis, I wonder if the farmers of western Canada are willing to accept I.O.U.'s for their products? It is obvious that trade could not be conducted on that basis, because the farmers could not afford it. When you bring it to the state level, the question arises whether the state

is in a position to extend further free loans to Great Britain for the purchase of agricultural products.
I have noticed that the leader of the C.C.F. party has never at any time, nor have any of his supporters when dealing with this question, referred to an interest-free loan to the United Kingdom. They have phrased it as accepting sterling in payment for our goods. So, Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the difficulty is the one experienced by many countries throughout the world, the exchange of goods for dollars. This was particularly true before devaluation of the British pound, because then the difficulty was that the British were more or less priced out of the United States market. Under those conditions, to suggest the trading of goods for goods leaves us with the same difficulty, because, for example, no one would trade two horses for one horse.
The official opposition, our Progressive Conservative friends, have taken a dangerously careless attitude, in my estimation. I believe they are completely blind to reality in their attitude towards increasing our exports to Great Britain. Our Progressive Conservative friends tell us that we ought to increase our markets in the United Kingdom, irrespective of the cost. Again and again they have referred to the United States as an unreliable market, as something that is meaningless, the importance of which can be dismissed by a wave of the hand. My main reason for participating in this debate is to counteract the idea that the market to the south of us is really unimportant.
The member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), in one of his speeches, referred to the United States as a country that produces the same type of surpluses we produce. There have been numerous speeches to that effect. I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce entitled "Foreign Trade", under date of February 4, 1950. It contains a summary of Canadian exports for the year 1949 which is quite revealing. It says:
Canadian exports to the United States last year had a value of $1,503-5 million, which represents an increase of 0-16 per cent over that for 1948.
We must compare that with our export trade with the United Kingdom. This publication goes on to say:
Exports to the United Kingdom, Canada's second largest customer, were valued at $705 million, representing an increase of 2-63 per cent over the figure for 1948.
There you have a comparison of the two markets so far as Canada is concerned. It is interesting to note that the increase in our exports to the United Kingdom amounted to
Agricultural Products Aci 2-6 per cent. An hon. member behind me asks whether that is losing markets. I recognize that markets for certain types of products have been lost, but the over-all picture for last year shows that our export trade with Great Britain increased 2-6 per cent. Our export trade with the United States also increased, but only by [DOT] 16 per cent.
I still say that the market to the south of us is certainly the most important market. At this stage we should make every effort to increase our trade with the United Kingdom, particularly for agricultural products, but at the same time we must be careful not to do anything to harm the United States market. Whether we like it or not, the logical market for Canada lies in the United States. Unlike the member for Dufferin-Simcoe, who said that we should look east and west and forget about north and south, I say that we should look east and west, but we should be careful to look south as well. In that direction lies the best customer we have had in the past few years. We should not discriminate against the United States market. We were forced to do it; but fortunately our very good friends to the south were broad-minded enough to realize our difficulties and to understand the situation. Instead of retaliating, they have helped us further to overcome our difficulties. That is real friendship and real international co-operation. We have every reason to be thankful for what the United States people have done for us.
At this stage I repeat that in our dealings and in our efforts to increase our market with Great Britain, we should at the same time be very careful to allow no discrimination to intervene against the United States.
In the publication to which I have referred there is another interesting quotation which reads:
Despite the over-all decline in exports from 1948 levels, three of the nine main commodity groups showed higher export values in the past year. These were the agricultural products group, which rose by 20-1 per cent to reach a total of $773 million.
Actually, therefore, in 1949 there was an increase in the export values of the agricultural products group. To continue:
In the first of these groups, the increase was due to a larger volume of wheat exports at higher average prices than in 1948. These reached $435-2 million, as opposed to $243 million in 1948.
There is the real picture; there are the real facts as they stare us in the face. The actual figure in 1949 was $435 million as against $243 million in 1948. Yet we had member after member on the opposition benches rising in his place and telling us that we are losing all our markets, and that we are heading for certain doom in the years to come.

Agricultural Products Act
As I said, taking the over-all picture, the United States market, generally speaking, is our best market. We have yet to explore all the possibilities in that market. We know for a fact that so far as cattle are concerned it is a market that is advantageous to Canada. At the present time, owing to various factors, many of our agricultural products are not allowed to go freely to the United States. I am not going to enter into that phase of it, because it is a complex one. But I do not think it is fair or true to say that the Canadian government is keeping those products under permit merely to protect the British market, or, as has been said, that the government is doing it to keep the price of agricultural products down. Of course this might have been true during the war, but it is certainly not true today. That is not the reason at all for many of these products being kept under permit. The only reason for their being kept under permit is that in these various lines there is a danger that if we were to send all our surpluses of those products into the United States they would probably go to a region in which there is already a surplus, and it would have a bad effect. There would be a demand in the United States to prohibit the entry of those products into that country; therefore permits are required, and the products are distributed in areas in which a surplus does not exist. We are allowed to carry on on that basis. It has proved beneficial in the past; but still the fact remains that we do not know exactly what the possibilities might be, because there has never been a free exchange of these particular products.
I know that so far the Canadian government have always been careful not to do anything that would harm the United States market, and I am sure they will not take the observations of our Conservative and C.C.F. friends too literally or too seriously, and will continue to use sound judgment, as they have in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill to amend the Agricultural Products Act, because I do not quite agree with the minister's interpretation of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright).
We in this group support the principle of the bill. We are going to vote for the bill when the vote is taken, but we believe in the terms of the amendment, namely,
That Bill No. 16 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introducing of a permanent agricultural products export act which would provide for the setting up of an export board, to fill present contracts, negotiate future contracts, and develop new markets abroad for surplus agricultural products.

My few references to this bill will be with respect to the fruit industry, to which this bill is a matter of serious concern. The growers have done everything they can in the way of production. There are few problems so far as production is concerned. There are few problems in connection with the preparation of the product for market. They have done all they can so far as organization is concerned. They have an active organization, all within the power of the growers. The prospects for continued prosperity in the fruit industry depend entirely upon a good proportion of the crop being exported overseas. I believe the minister was correct in this sense, namely, that the other acts could be used- the Agricultural Products Marketing Act is one-if we were living under normal conditions, or what are termed normal conditions, with regard to export markets. The producer boards could organize export in the regular trade channels; but we are asking for this amendment to the act because of agricultural surpluses created by abnormal world conditions.
We do not think that sectional organizations or producers' boards can market surplus agricultural products satisfactorily under the Agricultural Products Marketing Act, when we are facing a condition under which governments have to deal with varying exchange rates, international organizations such as the food and agricultural organization, the possibility of supporting the proposals made for an international commodities clearing house, and so on. In the opinion of the members of this group, that is beyond the capacity of the ordinary fruit producers' board or the legislation found in the Agricultural Products Marketing Act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are putting this amendment forward in the hope that the house will give it consideration, because we believe that if the house does accept it we shall have introduced into the bill some teeth that will make it possible for the government, with the other legislation, to take effective action with regard to the marketing of agricultural surpluses which now exist and without any doubt are likely to exist in the days ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), because I too am interested in the fruit industry. I am particularly interested in this amendment, because it is something that would place our industry on a sound and solid basis, with someone to go. to, someone to deal with effectively, in the matter of the disposition of fruit surpluses.
We know that a great deal can be done. Recently we read that the Minister of Trade

and Commerce (Mr. Howe), visited England and came back in the matter of a couple of weeks with $25 million in orders.
If we had someone on a permanent basis, with the same power, to go to Europe, to New Zealand and Australia, to travel the world seeing markets as the minister did on that occasion, then I could see a future for our Canadian surpluses. I have in mind the fact that New Zealand, facing a similar problem, where their great difficulty was one of distance, overcame it by setting up import-export boards to find markets and to get commodities to shipping points in the cheapest and best way. Then they proceeded to sell those commodities abroad, as government units. They were successful in finding markets at distances double those confronting us in Canada. They sold in Europe, and were able to establish sound foreign markets for their agricultural products, particularly butter. We in Canada could learn a great deal from their success.
I urge the minister and the house to consider seriously the amendment suggested by this group. Otherwise nearly half our crop is at the mercy of conditions which, if they continue, may make it necessary for us to dump or destroy those commodities, or give them away, as we have done this year.
While I am not condemning the bill- indeed, I support it-I urge upon the house consideration of the amendment in order to give the measure now before us a permanent and sound life, so that we may build up an industry which is handicapped by the length of time it takes to develop it-fifteen years; this no one can change. I wish to seek a permanent solution, and the only permanent solution is to make this act a permanent one.

Mr. Speaker, I rise, not so much to speak regarding the policies of the government, but more because of the criticism we have heard.
My constituency is mostly agricultural. We raise hogs and cattle, but our chief occupation is that of raising grain. When we have markets and receive good prices, because of the fact that we have few crop failures we have a reasonable degree of prosperity. I believe however that because we are producers of food the government will see to it that we will receive fair floor prices, so that we may be able to carry on. In my view, unless the producer is prosperous, no one else will be. If the farmer is not able to buy the products of labour it is not long before labour is out on the street.
_ Because I am a farmer I am naturally interested in the action taken by the government with respect to floor prices. If the farmers are to be given confidence in the
55946-74J
Agricultural Products Act future, we must have price support. If that support is not given there will be a greater flow of farmers to the cities, with the consequence that the unemployment situation will become worse. Today farmers cannot go into the labour market and obtain help, because most labourers do not care to go to the farms to work long hours for seven days a week. I believe however that labour and all other organizations will get behind this program of price support so as to keep our economy operating on the present scale. Workers will not enjoy shorter hours and good pay if the production of our farmers falls off to any considerable extent.
Farmers can tighten their belts to some degree, but there is the possibility that they may become discouraged and quit. The older folks may stay on the farms and raise enough for their own use, but certainly the younger folk will not. They will not stay on those farms, if other fields look greener. If we can maintain employment at its present level we will have a good market at home for our farm products. The home market is our best market. Even if we have some surpluses, surely that is better than to have scarcities. I believe, too, that labour and others will not complain too much about our program of price support if only they can keep up the level of employment and hold their jobs.
How are we going to keep farmers on the land? The only way I see in which it can be done is to give those farmers something to look forward to. Hon. members will know that the farmer is engaged in an occupation in which there are many hazards such as weather, drought, hail, grasshoppers and the like. If one more hazard is put in his path it may be just one too many, with the result that the farmers will leave the land to try something else.
I believe that on the whole our farming population is well satisfied with the way the government has handled our products in the past. Most cf the credit for this should go to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The opposition, both in this session and the last one, have tried to discredit the efforts of the minister. The fact remains however that when he was sick last fall those farmers were worried, and were wondering who could do a better job than he has done.
On many occasions our wheat policy has been criticized. I know of nothing that has been more universally accepted by western farmers than has this policy, and we want it continued. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has criticized the last payment on wheat of twenty cents per bushel. His criticism dealt particularly with the comparatively small amount of interest that had to be paid

The fact that most members of the opposition are now trying to run away from this *criticism indicates that they believe the government has done a good job in paying out this amount of money, instead of leaving it to accumulate in the banks at a time when the farmers in dried-out areas were in such need. I know opposition members have to look for something concerning which they can criticize the government, but I suggest they should not have criticized this action, particularly when about one hundred per cent of the farmers are in favour of it.
Let me say as a farmer that the comparatively small amount we paid for interest on loans to make this twenty-cent payment does not bother me. But when it comes to future wheat payments or future markets, then I might have some anxiety. It is not that I blame the government because this is one thing over which they have not very much control. Certainly the government cannot be blamed for what happens in other countries.
Then I do not think we should be too critical about what happens in other countries because those countries are trying to do what they think is best for their people. If we try to meet them with the idea or intention of helping them in their predicament,


then I believe something can be accomplished. We should let them know that we are anxious to help them out of their difficulties.
Surely if we know how to produce we should be able to find some way to distribute our surpluses. If we have small surpluses in certain cases, surely that is better than to have scarcities. Even with these floor prices I do think the government should let the markets carry themselves as far as possible. If there should be small surpluses at the end of the year I believe the government can well take care of them. When the $200 million fund is used over a period of years for this purpose there would be little loss.
We have to trade with the world, but it has to be a two-way market, or a twenty-way market as the minister said. The Canadian people have to be taught the fundamentals of trade. We have to take some goods for our own good because some day this trade will have to be equalized or balanced.
A word about home prices. Why should small export surpluses set the prices for our home market? The home labour market is not set by overseas wages, so why should the farmer's prices at home be set by competitive world prices? What is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander.
How are we going to get contracts?' It takes two parties to make an agreement and all agreements will have to be on terms advantageous to both parties. During the war the price of wheat to the consumer was held down, so is it not only fair that the consumer should pay a fair price for farm products? I am not pessimistic about the future as I believe we have learned a lot since the thirties.
On June 27 last this government received a definite vote of confidence from the people of Canada so I believe there will be little criticism when it passes legislation that is favourable to the producers. If the fifty per cent of our people who are producers are not prosperous, the other fifty per cent cannot be. I am sure the government realizes that fact and will act accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was objecting to the amendment moved by this group he said that we already had on the statute books an act which covered what is proposed to be covered by this amendment. The minister was referring to the Agricultural Products Marketing Act which was assented to on April 30, 1949. Section 2 of that act reads:
The governor in council may by order grant authority to any board or agency authorized under the law of any province to exercise powers of regulation in relation to the marketing of any agricultural product locally within the province, to regulate

the marketing of such agricultural product outside the province in interprovincial and export trade and for such purposes to exercise all or any powers like the powers exercisable by such board or agency in relation to the marketing of such agricultural product locally within the province.
I think it is clear that under that act the governor in council may give certain powers to provincial boards similar to those that can be granted within the province. But it does not envision, as does our amendment, the setting up of a federal export board to fulfil the present contracts, negotiate future contracts and develop new markets abroad for surplus agricultural products.
As the minister said, this act is just a temporary act. Apparently it was enacted on the assumption that our contracts will be on a temporary basis. Our amendment asks for the setting up of an export board which will negotiate future contracts on a permanent basis. That is what we expect to get back to this year, and any of our worries for the next year will start with October and go on into the next year.

If we are right in our calculations of the production for this year, which would be an increased production as compared with immediately preceding years, then we shall be taking a very considerable quantity of

speechtext: The minister said a few minutes ago that the government had 20 million pounds of cheese in storage. The statement I made a few moments ago was not that we have 20 million pounds in storage now. My hon. friend over here suggested that we had bought only 17 million pounds and I said we had bought over 20 million pounds in the year and now have somewhere between 17 million pounds and 20 million pounds in storage. That cheese has to be disposed of in some way. I understand that the question was whether we are going to use any of it to supply the British market. We have not determined that as yet.
We think at the moment-we may be right or wrong in this-that the Canadian people have not been great consumers of cheese largely because over the years that have gone by the poorest cheese has been palmed off on them while the best cheese has gone to the British market or elsewhere. There are some of us who think that we now have an opportunity of testing out this market with cheese that is well cured. If we do I hope we will get more than the British offered us for it. I said once before that I did not want to repeat the figure which was offered for the cheese some time around Christmas, but it was quite low. I am quite sure that unless we are able to get a little more than that for it none of it will go to Britain. We think we can sell it elsewhere, and our hope is that we can sell a lot of it in Canada.
The other question had to do with the market in the southern states. We have not been too successful there. When the British thought they could not get sufficient cheese from us last year they bought the surplus United States cheese which increased the price in the United States for a time. My understanding is that they now have considerable cheese. As I say, we have not been successful in attempting to market cheese there. On one or two occasions we have been in the position where we probably could have turned over some of that cheese at a price lower than we had paid for it. Someone might have made some money selling the cheese in the United States, but we do not think that that should be our objective. We think our objective should be to maintain the price of Canadian cheese at as high a level as we can and if possible to encourage the consumption of cheese in Canada. We hope

to utilize cheese which we think is good cheese for the purpose of trying to encourage that consumption.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF OPERATION FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR
speechtext: I realize that most of our cheese is produced in eastern Canada. In western Canada the dairy people produce butter rather than cheese. They have an investment, and the fact that there is a guaranteed price for butter is not sufficient to keep them in business if the manufacture of oleomargarine is finally going to undermine them. It would be helpful to these dairy people if the minister could tell them what the campaign he intends to promote may consist of, or whether legislation is proposed. In all seriousness, may I say that it would be most helpful to dairy people west of the great lakes if they could be given a lead along this line. As I say, I am mindful of the fact that many farmers use oleomargarine.

I appreciate your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I only wanted to make a few brief remarks about the other matter in passing. We of the Conservative party have always been in favour of legislation similar to that which is before us now. As I have stated before in the house, it was originally the policy of our party. We have no actual criticism of the principle of the bill except that the original act does not fix any formula for setting floor prices. Everything is left to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). In other words, he might still want to have a finger in the control. He cannot tell us how the present floor prices were arrived at except by the juggling of figures. There is no definite plan to relate it, in any way, to the farmers' costs. That is obvious, because their costs have not gone down, while floor prices have.
It is absolutely ridiculous and meaningless for the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to endeavour to create the impression that Canadian farmers are receiving higher prices than farmers in any other


country in the world, unless in each case he also shows the relationship of those prices to domestic costs. Can the minister give parliament the facts upon which he based that statement? Just this morning we received in the mail the latest Searle Grain Company report, that of Wednesday, March 22, from which I want to read one paragraph on the back page:
Supported British Agriculture
British farmers are being supported at the moment at prices for their products considerably higher than the prices at which most farm products could be imported. The London Economist in its issue of February 18 asks this question:
''In the course of time, increasing quantities of food are likely to become available from overseas which can be paid for in sterling. Supposing that the cost of such food is (as on present trends it certainly will be) substantially lower than the prices being paid to British farmers, what course will the government of the day pursue? Will it stand by the promise to purchase the whole output of British agriculture at whatever the cost? Or will it plead a prior duty to keep down the cost of living, and force on British agriculture a sharp and unpleasant adjustment?"
I think that is enough to show the minister was wrong the other evening when he said the prices of our agricultural products were higher than those of any other country. This quotation plainly shows that the prices of agricultural products in Great Britain are higher than those same products can be bought for elsewhere. All the figures the minister quoted last Thursday were wholesale prices, not prices to the producer; and in many cases there is a tremendous difference. For instance, the minister quoted 42-3 cents per dozen as the low price for eggs in 1949. I know, as do many hon. members, that the price to producers for ungraded eggs went as low as 16 cents a dozen last December. The government now guarantees the wholesaler who purchased those eggs for 16 cents a dozen a price of 38 cents plus storage for grade A large, which is rather a nice profit. It makes one wonder for whom the minister is actually working, the producers of this country or the wholesalers. A conservative estimate would be that one-quarter of the entire economy of this country is directly dependent upon agriculture. If our agricultural economy is allowed to deteriorate, the result must be obvious.
The other evening when the minister was reading his 1944 speech in the house, at page 1043 of Hansard, he said:
I hope that our markets for farm products for a period of years, possibly two or three or more, for most of our products, will be sufficiently good that we shall be able to obtain a price which is comparable with the price we are now obtaining for our farm products of different kinds. If so, the board that is in existence during that period of time will be keeping a check on what is happening during that period, comparing it with what happened during the war period-

I stress these next words.
-and immediately there is any necessity for taking action in connection with any farm product, authority is given the board under this legislation to purchase a surplus of that farm product at the floor price which the government of the day considers to be a reasonable floor in the light of all the facts existing in connection with the case.
Was that the situation when the floor price for eggs was fixed last fall or this spring? I do not think it was, because the government waited practically a month and a half before the floor of 38 cents was fixed. Certainly that is not "immediately." Then, in the same speech the minister quoted, he said:
Then I should say it would be unfair to the farmer immediately to require him to sell at the cost of production, without considering at all any losses he sustained because of the war or any returns he was denied through the controls established during the war. The suggestion was made that farmers had been denied returns in the earlier part of the war and that just at the time when in the ordinary course of events according to the experiences of the last war, he would have reaped some returns which would have been helpful to him, ceilings were placed upon prices, as a result of which he was denied as great a return as otherwise he might have received. All those matters would have to be taken into consideration during the transition period along the lines I have suggested.
Then, speaking over the radio from Niagara Falls on Monday, January 30, taking part in the national farm radio forum, he answered a question asked by Mr. Roy Marler of Alberta:

speechtext: I would like to direct my question to Hon. Mr. Gardiner. My question is "What basis or formula does the government use in arriving at a support price?"

In the matter of arriving at a support price, we follow the plan or idea which was laid down in 1944 when we suggested that most of our farmers-at least as their opinions expressed in farm organizations-considered the years 1943-44 as very satisfactory from the standpoint of returns as compared with costs, and we estimated that 1945 would be a similar year. We hoped at that time the war would end in 1945. The war did end in 1945 and our undertaking was that we would keep a record of the situation existing-that is, the relationship between farm prices and farm costs in the last three years of the war; and through the transitional period, we would attempt to keep the returns to the farmers in that fair relationship to the cost of the products they had to buy. That, generally speaking, is the plan and formula.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would say it was very generally speaking, with several ifs, ands and buts. Last Thursday evening the minister quoted the low price for eggs in 1949 as 42-3 cents. I find that the price in January, 1943, was 37 cents a dozen; in February, 36 cents; in March, 34 cents; and from April 20 it was 35 cents. In 1944 the price was 35J cents a dozen, and for 1945 it was 39 cents in the spring and 44 cents in the fall, with fresh eggs at 48 cents, fall storage. Then if we take

Mr. Speaker, the principle in the bill before us is quite simple. It asks that the Agricultural Prices Support Act be continued after March 31 of this year. I believe it is quite obvious to everyone that legislation is needed that will enable the government to place floor prices under farm products. During the last 15 or 16 months Canada has witnessed, as has the United States, a severe drop in farm income. Unless the government has legislation such as the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and unless the legislation is used in the proper manner, then there are sorry times ahead for the agricultural industry.
The farmers of this country are looking to the federal government to establish adequate floor prices under the main agricultural commodities. They believe that the low prices which have come about in the last few months have resulted directly from the policy this government has followed since the war. That being so, they are looking to this government to set proper floor prices. It is admitted by the government, and has' been admitted by it since the end of the war, that the government does not believe in contracts for agricultural products on a permanent basis. I shall repeat it, and it can be substantiated by a reading of the preamble of the Agricultural Products Act, under which the government fulfils the contract.

Agricultural Prices Support Act I have not the preamble before me, but I think the minister will agree that the Agricultural Products Act was set up under the Transitional Measures Act. When the minister comes before this house and says there is still an emergency resulting from the war and we should, therefore, pass this act for another year, he is saying that contracts are not going to be undertaken on a permanent basis. If the government were really anxious to inaugurate contracts for the sale of agricultural products year in and year out, it would bring in a permanent act, instead of asking us to extend the Agricultural Products Act from year to year under this emergency powers legislation.
I say, too, that if this government believed in bilateral contracts and the bilateral method of trading, then the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would not have denied that the government would undertake such contracts. It would not have been necessary, if this government believed in the bilateral method of trading, for the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) to amend what I considered was an excellent speech, in which he advocated bilateral agreements. The difficulty in which we, as a nation, find ourselves is that, in spite of what the member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) said, I still consider Great Britain is our best market. Great Britain believes in bilateral contracts not only for exporting goods but also for importing goods. Because the British believe in that method of trading, and because this government does not believe in it, we find we have already lost a substantial portion of the British market for many farm commodities.
For example, while we shipped approximately 65 million pounds of bacon to Britain last year, under these bilateral agreements Britain purchased 20 million pounds from the Netherlands, 40 million pounds from Eire, and 40 million pounds from Poland. Under that contract, she may buy as high as 120 million pounds. Britain bought 100 million pounds of bacon under bilateral contracts and in addition took 90 per cent of the Danish surplus. While we supplied about 65 million pounds of bacon, Britain had contracts for the purchase of 200 million pounds.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to point out some of the need that has arisen for a support 
act, and why at this time a support act, with proper floors, was absolutely necessary. I had placed some figures on Hansard to show how we were losing the British market, and that the people of Great Britain had been able successfully, through bilateral trade agreements, to obtain large quantities of bacon from countries other than Canada.
In order to show how serious has been our loss of the British market for bacon, I might point out that back in the year 1938 Canada shipped to Great Britain 189 million pounds of bacon, whereas this year we are hoping to ship not more than 60 million pounds. This year the total value of our bacon contract is some $17,500,000; whereas in 1938, a year when we were just emerging from a depression, the value of .the bacon shipped to Great Britain was $32 million, or almost twice as much as the present contract.
Policies adopted by this and other governments certainly affect the chances we have of selling our commodities in the European markets. As has already been pointed out, the devaluation of the British pound has made it more difficult for Canada to export agricultural commodities to that market. I might say that when the British made the decision to devalue the pound it was not because they wanted to, but out of sheer necessity. In my opinion devaluation of the pound was brought about largely because of the failure of Canada and the United States to purchase adequate imports from Great Britain. Because that is so, and because devaluation followed, we find a reduction in the price of bacon and of cheese under our contracts. The bacon contract price is reduced from $36 a hundredweight last year to $29 this year, almost the exact amount brought about through devaluation.
We in this group have always supported the United Nations, and the various bodies set up under the United Nations. We support the FAO, and we were sorry that when they proposed an international commodity clearing house arrangement for the disposal of surplus foods in the world's market our government, through our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), found it impossible to support that arrangement. Because of that, and because of the other factors that I have mentioned, we have the problem of disposing of agricultural surpluses. In my opinion that problem has been brought about largely because of the various policies adopted by the government since the conclusion of the war.
In his speech this afternoon the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), as did the Minister of Agriculture last Thursday,

emphasized the value of the United States market. Both the hon. member for Pro-vencher and the minister made the statement that the United States is our second best market. While the United States may be our second best market for many commodities, in my opinion that country is not our second best market for most agricultural products. 1 agree that the first and most important market is our own Canadian market; but in my opinion after that the United Kingdom offers the opportunity of a permanent market for most of our agricultural products whereas the United States does not offer that type of market.
At the present time the United States has, according to the Ottawa Citizen of March 10, almost $4 billion invested in agricultural surpluses held by the government. In looking over the list of agricultural surpluses one finds that a great many of the surpluses in the United States are identical with the surpluses we have in Canada. According to that article the United States has 100 million pounds of butter held by the government, and 25 million pounds of cheese, both commodities that Canada has had some difficulty in disposing of at 1949 prices. The United States has 52 million bushels of barley on hand held by the government, and some 627 million bushels of corn. While the United States does provide a market for surplus Canadian cattle, I do not think that country is likely to provide an effective market for Canadian hogs if after the conclusion of the present agreement with Britain no other agreement is signed.
While the United States government does not hold hogs in surplus supply, nevertheless the 627 million bushels of corn and the 52 million bushels of barley could be converted into hogs in a very short time. One cannot see that the United States is likely to provide a market for Canadian wheat, although I do know that in his speech to the FAO conference last fall the Minister of Agriculture said that he hoped the United States would lift the embargo on Canadian wheat. Whether the United States will lift that embargo I do not know, but judging by the surpluses of wheat they hold, I am afraid that such a move would be of very little value to Canada.
According to the article to which I have referred, the United States has invested over $1 billion in wheat. The United States surplus of wheat held by the government amounts to some 475 million bushels. Therefore I do not feel that the United States will provide a market for Canadian wheat.
In the last few weeks and months we have seen a drop in many agricultural food commodities produced in Canada. At the same time we do know that the prices of coarse
Agricultural Prices Support Act grains, such as oats and barley, are still high. No. 1 feed oats was being sold by the wheat board on Thursday, March 23, at 96 cents a bushel. No. 1 feed barley was being sold by the wheat board for $1.35J a bushel. I believe that these prices for oats and barley are high in relation to the new prices established for bacon, eggs and other agricultural products. I do not suggest that the price of oats or barley should be reduced in any way. I hope that these prices will not fall, but when I read in the press that the Minister of Agriculture was suggesting to western farmers that they reduce their wheat acreage this year by three million acres I was wondering whether he did not know that such a reduction in wheat acreage would mean an increase in the acreages of oats and barley. If there is an increase in the production of oats and barley, with the present support prices under bacon and eggs and cheese at existing low levels, then in my opinion it is inevitable that oats and barley prices will fall.
So I say the government, through the floor prices it has adopted, through the suggestion that three million acres be taken out of wheat production-and as a result, of course, most of it will go into the production of something else, probably oats and barley, with increased supplies-is expecting a lowering of the whole level of agricultural products.
If that is the policy of the government, as it seems to be, then I certainly object to it in the strongest terms. I did not expect under this measure any lowering of prices for various agricultural commodities during the present year. The Minister of Agriculture, as reported at page 1043 of Hansard for March 23, repeated a speech he made when introducing the Agricultural Prices Support Act in 1944. In that speech he said this:
Then I should say it would be unfair to the farmer immediately to require him to sell at the cost of production, without considering at all any losses he sustained because of the war or any returns he was denied through the controls established during the war. The suggestion was made that farmers had been denied returns in the earlier part cf the war and that just at the time when in the ordinary course of events according to the experiences of the last war, he would have reaped some returns which would have been helpful to him, ceilings were placed upon prices, as a result of which he was denied as great a return as otherwise he might have received. All those matters would have to be taken into consideration during the transition period along the lines I have suggested.
I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture could have considered the hundreds of millions of dollars of income the farmers of this country have been denied because of the government's policy over the last few years, when it was dropping the prices of bacon, cheese and eggs? Surely if the farmers are
1156	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Prices Support Act to receive something extra because of the money that was denied them, then floor prices should not drop. Floor prices should be held at the level prevailing in 1949, so that part of the money denied the farmers in the last few years could be made up to them.
I object that the bill as it now stands does not in any definite way set floor prices under agricultural products from year to year whereby the farmer can know in advance what floor prices will be. The other night the Minister of Agriculture reviewed some of the discussions which had taken place at the convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at Niagara Falls. He suggested in that speech that before Canadian floor prices were established he and his officers checked on the period 1943, 1944 and 1945. He made the statement in that speech that Mr. Galbraith, an economist from the United States, I believe,. informed the convention that the basis of parity in that country was for the period from 1909 to 1914, and that that period was a good deal lower than the Canadian period of from 1943 to 1945.
_ The minister quoted Mr. Galbraith as having said that the United States period was in the neighbourhood of 15 per cent lower than the Canadian period. Then the minister quoted Dr. Hope, Canadian Federation of Agriculture economist, as having been surprised that the Canadian period was higher than the period accepted in the United States. Then the minister makes this statement, in reference to Dr. Hope:
He did not say how much better, but he said it was better in Canada. In other words, our base is the highest price.
Well, Mr. Speaker, our base may be the highest price, but our base is not in legislative form. And our base, as used by the Minister of Agriculture, is only a base on which the government checks. Apparently it checks on that base, and then it sets a price lower than the base. It may be just as advisable-
I do not know-to check on the base period in the early thirties, when prices were very low, and then, instead of giving that base period as the established price, set a price a good deal higher.
It is not enough to have a base period on which you are merely checking. If the Agricultural Prices Support Act is to mean anything, then the price relationship prevailing in the base period should be written into the act, and that should be the price below which farm commodities are not allowed to fall.
At this point I should like to quote from an article issued by the Michigan state college extension service, department of agricultural economics, at East Lansing, Michigan. This article is written by Mr. Arthur Mauch, and


in it he points out the method used in the United States in the setting of floor prices. For 1950, under the basic crops, there is established a floor at 90 per cent of parity, and the basic floor under dairy products must be established at something between 75 per cent and 90 per cent of parity, according to the statute.
Then on the next page of the same article it sets out the various floors for 1950 for agricultural products in the United States, and shows that the United States formula arrives at a basic floor price for wheat of $2.12 a bushel; for butterfat, 63 cents a pound-5 cents higher than the present Canadian floor price under butter, and probably a good deal higher than the floor the minister may announce in a few days. I hope I am wrong in my assumption on that score. This table indicates that the floor in the United States under eggs is 51-6 cents a dozen, whereas the floor under Canadian eggs based, as the minister inferred, on the highest base period, is one of 36 or 38 cents a dozen. The floor under oats in the United States is 95 cents a bushel, as compared with the Canadian floor of 61J cents; that under barley in the United States is $1.49 as compared with the Canadian floor of about 90 cents.
So, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize again that it is not enough to have a measure like this before the House of Commons. It is not enough for the minister to say, "We have a certain base period, and we are checking on that base period"-if after he checks on the base period he does not establish floors equal to the prices prevailing in that base period.
While the United States base period may not be as high as some other periods, nevertheless the actual floor prices adopted in that country by their formula are a good deal higher than the prices established in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in this debate. On Thursday last when the two resolutions were introduced we thought it would be advisable to hasten their passage through the house, but at this stage I desire to point out certain things which I feel are necessary in this type of legislation. I think all of us recall quite well the promises that were made in 1945 and 1949 with regard to the Agricultural Prices Support Act. We all know that there was a $200 million revolving fund set up under the act.
I think members of the house agree with the general principle of this act, but the workings of the act have certainly not come up to the expectations of the primary producers across this country. I agree with the statements made on the resolution stage by my colleague, the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton), and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). I think most primary producers welcomed the legislation because it was heralded as a step in the stabilization of prices by which they would know from month to month what they were going to get for their products when they planted them; but that has not been the result so far.
I think we all support this legislation because of the degree of stability it will bring to labour and industry. Unless the purchasing power of the primary producers is maintained it will not be long before the men in the cities will be looking for jobs. That has been demonstrated definitely during the past few months. As the prices of farm products
27, 1950
Agricultural Prices Support Act dropped, the number of unemployed increased. It is only reasonable to expect that, because it is the purchasing power of the primary producers of this country that keeps the wheels of industry turning.
As I say, the application of the act so far has been disappointing. As far as eggs are concerned there has been too little too late. That is not what the farmers voted for in 1949. Did it provide stability for hogs? It did after a large number of producers had suffered considerable losses through not knowing where prices were going. It took the government so long to make up their minds where they were going to set the prices and the result was losses for a number of producers.
Did it provide stability for butter? Only after the horse was stolen. Did it provide stability for honey? The price of honey is down to where it was in 1900. Did it provide stability for beans? Only in a very precarious way because the bean producers themselves provided the greatest amount of stabilization in the marketing of their commodity.
We need a realistic approach to this problem of agricultural prices support. Those prices should be arrived at by a definitely known formula. They should be arrived at after consultation with the various commodity groups that know something about the cost of production and the labour factors that go into the production of their particular product.
The prices support should be clear and be directly applicable to the primary producer rather than to the wholesale trade. We have seen the results of that so far as eggs are concerned. The wholesale trade can take care of themselves in all these changes that are taking place. It is the primary producer who gets the squeeze every time and therefore any floor prices legislation should be based on a scheme that will definitely assure the primary producer what he is going to get, not the wholesaler or the middleman.
I repeat that we require a workable formula, not one based on political expediency. In the past we have seen what political prices can mean to farm products. That is one reason why I opposed the amendment to Bill No. 16. I was afraid that the price that would be paid for goods that were requisitioned would have no relation to the cost of production or to the purchasing power that those particular goods might represent for the purchase of the products of industry and labour. We do not want a "tick, tack, toe, here I go" system of picking out what the price support legislation is going to be and the prices thereunder. Taking what it was last year, we do not want a guess as to what it might be next year. That is not good enough.

Agricultural Prices Support Act That is not what the farmers voted for. We want a formula based on the needs of Canada, on the needs of Canadian markets and the consuming public, because after all the home market is the greatest potential market we have. It should be based on reality, cost of production, purchasing power, and last of all, but most important, on the idea of maintaining the economy of the country because when the time arrives that primary producers are accepting 25 per cent less for their products than they have been, you are going to have unemployment and a decrease in income so far as the government in concerned. Income tax collections will fall as will sales tax receipts and with the expenditures to which this country is now committed you will find yourselves in a very serious situation.
The cabinet is the board of directors of the nation, a crown company in a sense. During the war they made certain promises to the producers that when the war was over they would be protected so far as their prices were concerned. Now some members of the cabinet are saying that conditions have changed and that we cannot now carry on with the program outlined at that time. When a company fails to carry out its promises or to honour its promissory notes it goes bankrupt and liquidation proceedings take place. That is just what will happen to this government if it does not carry out its promises to the primary producers. There will be a liquidation.
During the war years the primary producers contributed a very large sum of money to the maintenance of stable prices in Canada on the promise that when the war was over they would be taken care of. Now the government is reneging on its promise. Why do we ask for these particular safeguards? To ensure purchasing power in the hands of Canadian citizens who will continue to buy our products. The purchase of Canadian products will bring about increased employment. One thing that is bothering everyone in Canada today is the threat of greater numbers of unemployed in all our cities. If the purchasing power of the primary producers is reduced you will have more unemployment instead of less.
Recently the newspapers carried headlines regarding the rapid action taken by the government to protect the shirt and glove industry of Canada from competition with low-priced goods produced in other countries. They were not in as great a hurry to protect our primary producers from competition with low-cost products brought in from foreign lands. If it is good for one it is good for the other. It is quite possible that the farmer and the labourer might like to get a cheap shirt once in a while. The creation of a floor price formula should not be delayed until producers
fMr. White (Middlesex East).]

are discouraged, dismayed, or better still- mark my words, "better still" not "worse still" -fighting mad about it, because that will be all to our advantage. Again I say that while this legislation is not all that we would wish for, we welcome its introduction and hope that the amendments suggested will be carried out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to rise again this evening on these measures. However, the two bills are so closely related that I should like to make a few observations on the Agricultural Prices Support Act. First of all, we have heard a great deal, particularly during the resolution stage, about agricultural surpluses in Canada. It is a fact that for a great many years we have had the problem of agricultural surpluses, and apparently we will continue to have it for a few years to come. I was amazed at the attitude of the C.C.F. party as to these surpluses. If you will look at Hansard you will see at page 1047 the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) had this to say with reference to surpluses:
It is not right, it is not just, that we should be piling up surpluses of agricultural commodities in Canada when there are hungry people in the world.
Again and again during the debate, various members of the opposition have referred to our surpluses. They have pointed to them as if it were wrong for Canada to have surpluses, and have even almost insinuated that there was something wrong with our economic system, something wrong with our system altogether that we should have such large surpluses in Canada when there were people starving in other parts of the world. I suggest that if we have large surpluses in Canada it is largely due to our system of government, our economic system, our system of free enterprise. Instead of something that should be looked upon as bad it is one of the best tributes that can be paid to our free enterprise system. There is no question that some countries in Europe have suffered destruction because of the war, but the same cannot be said of some other countries where people are starving but which did not experience the war at all. We have developed one of the most efficient systems, and when I say "we" I refer to the North American continent. We should be proud of it. Of course it raises certain problems. We have surpluses and the question is how to distribute them. At page 1052 of Hansard the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) said:
Obviously then, Mr. Speaker, our problem is one of distribution.
He would make it appear that the only problem involved is one of distributing our surplus goods. Of course when we go to the

bottom of the matter it is much more involved than just the question of distribution. Fundamentally it is not a question of distribution but a question of production. We know that in most of these underdeveloped countries, where people are in need of our surplus products, if their production reached the same level as ours we should have no difficulty in sending our goods to them. Therefore it is much more a question of the lack of production in other countries than a question of distribution. Be that as it may, we have this problem, and we will have it for some time yet.
Reference has been made to the many plans put forward to take care of the situation, including the Brannan plan, the ICCH plan, and I believe the Dr. Hope plan. In my humble opinion, however, none of these plans solves the basic problem. We have surpluses. People are starving in other countries. If our surpluses are to get to the people in other countries who cannot pay for them, that can be done in only one way; that is, we will have to give them away. If we give something away we get nothing in return for it, and somebody has to pay. Under the Brannan plan the taxpayer must pay for the charity that is extended. The ICCH plan is much the same thing, only at the international level. In considering this latter plan, which has been referred to by the C.C.F. party and particularly by the Social Credit group, who seem to place a great deal of faith in it, I would point out that under it Canada would be perhaps the country to suffer most. There is one problem for which a solution is not found in any of these plans; that is, a way to prevent the disposal of these surpluses from depressing prices throughout the country. As far as I know no one has found a satisfactory solution to that branch of the problem.
It is all very well to say we can depend upon the treasury to make up the difference, but we must realize that if the bill that must be paid by the taxpayers of Canada or any other country became too large, no government could possibly continue such a plan for any length of time. With prices depressed, you can imagine what would be the plight of the farmers throughout the country, so in the end the problem would be far worse than it was in the beginning. So I say that while there is a great deal of merit in all these plans, we must face the facts. If something is given away someone has to pay for it; there is no way around it. We must make up our minds whether or not we are in a position to do that. If we should go ahead with such a plan we will have to decide whether the producer or the taxpayer is to pay the difference, or whether it should be apportioned in some
27, 1950
Agricultural Prices Support Act other way. Basically the one thing we must face is that as long as it is a gift we cannot expect anything in return; so the cost must be borne by the people as a whole. It is all very well to say there is something wrong with our system of distribution because we have surpluses while other people are starving, but the matter is not so easily resolved, and we must face that fact sooner or later.
In the course of the discussion we have also heard from our C.C.F. friends a great deal of what I would call propaganda from their socialist friends in the United Kingdom. For a full day we had a recital of the wonderful things that have been done in the United Kingdom for the stability of agriculture, and we were told that conditions there were so much better than a few years ago. Well, I suggest to my hon. friends that instead of being so engrossed in their propaganda from overseas they should look around their own communities. Of course there have been great changes, in Canada as well as elsewhere. Compare the stability of agriculture in this country today with the position in the thirties. Compare the position of the farmer today with his position in the nineties. There has been a tremendous improvement, and that applies to most countries in the world. Everywhere there has been progress. A few years ago we heard all about Australia and New Zealand; now it is pretty well narrowed down to the United Kingdom, and they persist in spreading as much propaganda [DOT] as they can with regard to things done outside our own country.
It would seem, according to our friends, that all our problems may be solved by what they used to call a planned economy, by the stroke of a pen. That was the generality; that was supposed to be the cure-all. Of course we know the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan, which has had to face realities, now is not so keen as it was on this planned economy. As a matter of fact they are dropping their plans like hot cakes, and have got rid of most of their supposed planning experts. Our friends of the C.C.F. in this house have not had that unpleasant experience, however, so they can still play with these generalities. Last Thursday they came forward with a new slant, or what I might call a new catchword. It was referred to by the leader of the C.C.F. as "forward pricing arrangements," which I suppose is the new version of the planned economy. That is very general; I suppose it embraces practically all production, all marketing and what not. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), in his usual clear and straightforward

Agricultural Prices Support Act way, gave us a definition of what was meant by that terminology. He said, at page 1051 of Hansard:
I mean, by that that when we breed a cow we will know how much we will get for the steer three years hence.
That is supposed to be what the hon. member's leader called a forward pricing arrangement. Other speakers referred to the same subject, and they became so enthused over their discovery that when their leader had his turn he went still further and improved on the system. He said, at page 1064 of Hansard:
. . . they know what it will be four years in advance, even before the cow is bred.
If that is not a super-planning theory, I do not know what is. It just goes to show how easily our friends can be carried away.
We have before us at the moment an amendment moved by the C.C.F. group which, as far as I can understand it, asks that a formula be placed in the act. I for one will support the bill as it is. No doubt it is another step towards stabilizing agriculture in this country. It is the fulfilment of a promise that the government made. A good deal of criticism was heard to the effect that the government had not kept its promises. Here is a promise that was made which the government is attempting to keep, but which our friends are trying to prevent it from keeping, in spite of the complaints they have made.
This raises the question of the formula. I am willing to admit that there might be some good in the formula. Before supporting a formula, however, I would have to know what the formula contains. From the experience of the United States, and from our farm leaders in the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, we know that no matter what formula we adopt, that formula must be of necessity a most flexible one. It must be adaptable from time to time. That being the case, Mr. Speaker, it is hardly a formula, if it has to be changed and adapted, or if it is left to the minister to decide to what degree the formula will be applied. If we have to have a formula of that nature, I cannot see any difference between that and the policy the minister is now following. Inevitably all conditions at the time have to be taken into consideration. It would seem, therefore, just as well to leave the matter in the hands of the minister and the cabinet. They have told us what formula they are using. Even if we placed another formula in their hands, we would still have to allow them to interpret it.
Frankly, I cannot see the merit of the amendment that has been suggested to this bill. We know that this bill is welcomed by the farmers throughout Canada. As I said,
[Mr. Jutras.l
it is a step forward towards greater stability in agriculture. It is a step forward in the policy of this government. For the last few years this government has continuously tried to give a greater degree of stability to agriculture. I can say without fear of contradiction, and I said it during the last election campaign at all my meetings, that I doubt if in the history of this nation farmers ever had a better friend in any government than they have in this administration. The farmers realize it, Mr. Speaker. Since trust and confidence have to be placed in someone, they are quite prepared to leave it with the present Minister of Agriculture. I should have said that, of all the ministers of agriculture this country has known, certainly no minister has done more for agriculture and the stability of agriculture than the present minister. I doubt if anyone would attempt to deny that. His reputation in that regard is certainly well known.
I quite readily admit that some of the farm organizations, individual farmers and even ourselves, might occasionally prefer to have a set formula that could be applied mathematically, so we would definitely know where we were. Everyone realizes that that is not feasible, nor is it practical. Why get involved in more red tape, if we are going to end up the same way? I can understand my good friends in the C.C.F., because they have to plan and control everything. It is to be expected that they will press for any measure that will add more and more control, more and more planning. They do not believe in free enterprise. They do not believe in this system. They believe they can do everything better than the individual can do it. I am not surprised, therefore, that they should move this amendment. I do say it contributes very little, and I certainly propose to vote against it.
