Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few words at this time. The member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) has made an excellent speech, which consisted largely of telling us what a wonderful fellow the Minister of Agriculture is. I know that is true in certain things. He played a fair game of football, or soccer as we called it at one time. He has always made money out of his farm. By that, I mean he has made money by growing crops. Some farmers make money from their farms otherwise, but he is a real farmer and makes money by growing crops, and without any guarantees of the kind he now gives since he has become Minister of Agriculture.
I venture to make a suggestion which I think will be quite unpopular in the farming portion of the constituency in which I live.

I am going to say now that I am quite content for another year. That may indicate how I shall vote. I do think it is about time that this parliament ceased (to be operated by pressure groups. The farm group is one of the most important, and the labour pressure group is the other group.
I think it is about time that we members of parliament started to look after the consumer a little. After all, he is the fellow who pays the bills. He has no organization. He has no way of getting at us. We are met by all these other people of influence who are organized to the nth degree, and so make themselves felt.
Someone will say, of course, that having said what I have just said, I am opposed to maintaining prices in agriculture; that is not so. I am one of those who still think that agriculture is our main and sustaining industry. In the time which I have lived, I have learned from experience that when agriculture lags in income, the whole nation lags in income. I believe there is a definite connection between the two statements. New wealth, sir, comes in only one way. You first take a natural resource, in this case the land; to that land you apply capital and labour, and you get new wealth. It is obtained in no other way, irrespective of what that natural resource may be. From these resources comes every bit of our new wealth, and it is only new wealth that makes a country prosperous.
Suppose you and I come by some stocks on the market tomorrow. We may sell those stocks at a considerable profit, but we must remember that that profit would come from the man who owned them before. No new wealth would be created by those city slicker methods of getting money on the markets, or on land or on anything of that kind. Having said that, I am in favour of the maintenance of prices. The amendment says minimum prices; I think it really means ceiling prices when the thing is worked out. Having said that I cannot come back and deny my first broad statement. But I am going to say to you, sir, that the minute we take the economy of Canada and patch it here and there and elsewhere with floors and ceilings, the closer we come to the destruction of our whole economy.

I am going to give you even more than that in a minute. Tariffs were the beginning of the industrial era of this country. We must always remember that tariffs were first made by any country as a means of self-protection. In those days the idea of nations getting along with one another was never agitated for or even suggested. It may seem strange for me to say this because I stand where I do. After all the tinkering we have done with markets, and since we have grown industrially, I am very much in favour of letting our products and our money take their places in the world's markets. Let us find out what our products are worth, and what our money is worth. My thinking now is all along that particular line.
I am in favour of holding the prices support act, as called for in the bill. I think that if we quit playing with our economy, if we quit this patchwork business, and let our goods find their own level in world markets, the better it will be for Canada. I do not mean world markets of the kind we have established recently, for example, in coarse grains. I know that what I say now will be very unpopular with all those pools and farm organizations in western Canada, which have been operated on a basis of hatred for the Winnipeg grain exchange, hatred, selfishness-

Speak for
myself! I am speaking for myself, and if you are capable of speaking for yourself you will have plenty of opportunity tomorrow.
So long as greed and fear are motivating factors in human conduct-and in my judgment they are, and I think they always will be-requests will be made for special legislation. But it is time the dominion parliament and government stopped being a "gimme" organization every time we are approached by any group of our population who are seeking a handout here and there.
Why should we tie our prices in this agricultural matter to 1944-48? The answer is that it certainly suits the producers of farm products, because it was in that period that, if we did not reach the peak, we reached a very high level. You may think, sir, that I have been arguing against this legislation, but I come back to say this. I support the idea of the extension of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. But I say at the moment I am not prepared to commit myself to having this parliament saying about one product, or one related series of products, that we shall maintain a certain level. True the amendment saves itself by saying that the relationship shall be preserved. I am one of those who hope that it will be preserved. I am one of

Agricultural Prices Support Act those who know that in the country from which I come the farmers for a long time have had the short end of the stick. In other words, there was not any proper relationship between the prices they got for that which they produced and the prices they paid for that which they bought. I know that is a good slogan, but I wonder just how much it means. We say that in producing grain we get so much a bushel. Then we are told that the price of a binder or a combine in these modern days has been going up and up. But I have never had anyone yet tell me how many bushels of grain a binder will cut. I have never had anyone tell me how many bushels of grain a combine will cut and thresh. Until we look at the thing in that way we cannot make a comparison. We cannot just take the percentage of the rise in price, because we sell grain and produce every year. We buy a binder once every ten years and a combine in roughly the same time. Therefore in our thinking about these matters we must average the increase in the price of a farm implement over the period of time, and over the produce that it will process, if that is the proper word to use.
You may ask me, sir, where does the member for Calgary West stand on this thing. I am going to say that the principle of the relationship in our prices is more than a pious hope. It is something which is interrelated, very sound. We know that the farmer has got the worst of it in times gone by.
I now come back to the remark made by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I say to him that there is something in his question to me about tariffs. Tariffs are of two kinds. . As a matter of fact they were put on for the protection of Canadian industry. Just suppose I made tin dippers over here-I know this is beneath his dignity-and suppose the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made tin dippers over there, the gangway being the boundary between the two countries. A protective tariff was one which permitted me, and only permitted me, to be able to sell my tin dippers at the same price that he sold his, which were produced at a smaller cost because he had a tremendous marketing area compared with my small one. I think, sir, that those days have gone by. I refer to one particular company, the Massey-Harris Company. I remember years ago we had to protect Canadian implement companies; but today the Massey-Harris Company is one of the greatest sellers of farm implements in the United States of America. We all know that they practically saved American crops some two or three years ago by putting in their combines down near the gulf, working north and thereby practically saving the crop.

My point is this:	I think our industryand I am saying this in answer to what my hon. friend asked-I think our industry in many lines has achieved a place where it does not need governmental protection from anybody. I will go a little further and say that those people who cannot operate without protection should first look to their own internal economy, their own costs, so that they do not need the cushion of a tariff.
Free trade, you say? No. I realize there are many conditions entering into this. If your labour costs in an exporting country- and we import into this one-are away below those of our workmen, then certainly you have to have a tariff. Why? Not to protect the workmen as such, but to protect the great numbers of our population who are engaged in working, perhaps not in that industry, but in one way or another. Our duty here, obviously, is to do the greatest good for the greatest number of people within our dominion. I think the amendment is wrong in endeavouring to tie the Canadian economy whose fluctuations are many, and some of them very quick indeed-I think it is wrong to endeavour to tie that economy to a given area, 1944 to 1948, without regard to the many things which may and easily can happen.
So, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote for the amendment, because it is an advocacy of the principle of tying our agricultural economy to the rest of our industrial economy. And by that I mean this, that I think it is perfectly true that the farmers get too little of the income of Canada. That did increase -and in this particular period it almost reached parity, or in any event reached a point which was the nearest our farmers had ever come to it.
In view of that fact I am going to vote for the amendment. I do not like the 1944 to 1948 period or any other period being fixed as a yardstick; because we can find from the bureau of statistics in any year what proportion of the income those persons who were engaged in agriculture, having regard to the population, got, as compared with those persons who were otherwise engaged. So I am going to vote for the amendment in affirmation of the principle of a proper relationship between the economy of the farm and the rest of our economy-and for no other reason.

Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was out west recently warning the people of Alberta and the west to discontinue sending their cattle to the United States in such numbers. Men who lived during the days of 1918 and 1919 know what can happen. Many of us went through experiences that made us sweat blood. for one-half the hay we had put into the cattle during the year. Scores and scores of men who had produced beef cattle, many for as long as 25 years, were ruined utterly and have never recovered.

I say the time has come when farmers as the producers of the fundamental values of the nation must be protected against the attacks of well organized men who would destroy them if they had the chance. As the minister will argue-and correctly-the act is designed to give the farmer that sort of protection, and because it is so designed I support the minister in introducing the bill.
So far as I can see, there is no reason why there should not be a guarantee given for prices and markets in connection with all kinds of meats. I find in the October report of IFAP-I find it difficult to remember all these fantastic letter names-that there is not going to be any danger of a surplus of meats in the world so far as they can see. There is no serious prospect of surplus either in hard or soft currency areas for a number of commodities, e.g., meats other than pork.
They do not seem to be quite as hopeful about pork as they do about other meats, but I read that to indicate that we do not need to be afraid to encourage the production of meats if we are prepared to be wise in protecting the farmers' prices and markets.
As several members have already said, our greatest market is the home market in

Agricultural Prices Support Act Canada. We have not begun yet to use our home market. I suppose there are millions of people in Canada who are not in a position to have the beef they would like to eat, and a good many other fine things that the farmers are prepared to produce. These potential consumers in Canada can all be made actual consumers, the potential home market can be made an actual effective market, if wise measures are adopted in respect of the Canadian economy. These wise measures will be monetary. Later on I expect to quote the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to the effect that our troubles are monetary. The trouble with the home market, like all markets in so far as they obtain for Canada, is a lack of appropriate monetary measures.
As to foreign markets, what is the trouble there? The minister himself has made the statement quite definitely that the trouble with our foreign markets is a lack of correct monetary measures. There is something wrong with the money. I think I will quote the passage in which the minister wisely made that statement. In a speech which he made before the food and agricultural organization at Washington on November 25, 1949, he said:
Our monetary difficulties today threaten to reproduce the situation which existed twenty years ago, a lack of that free movement of food from those with food to spare to those in want.
That is perfectly correct.
Unless some way can he found of solving this problem, we cannot hope for that "all-out" effort by exporting countries that is needed, if the people of the whole world are to be adequately fed.
The minister there speaks just as though he were becoming a Social Crediter, as if he were beginning to see the vision of Social Credit which would be the greatest honour that the minister has had conferred on him in his life, because he would then be able to see the way out of our difficulties.
It is one thing to say there are difficulties. I am glad that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is in the house now and a bit merry because of what I have just said. It is one thing to say there are monetary difficulties and it is another thing to tell what to do to remove them. The problem confronting the Minister of Finance and the other members of the government is what to do about these monetary difficulties. Up to the present time there has not been a word from them to indicate that they know what to do.
I should like to deal for a minute or two with the matter of ICCH inasmuch as the hon. member for Provencher has brought it up in the debate. I can imagine that a great many people in the country would like to


know something about what it is. I should like to quote certain passages from this IFAP periodical of October to give the people who will be reading Hansard an idea of what ICCH is. On page 3 I find the following: ICCH should1 be constituted as a public corporation with a capital fund equivalent to $5 billion. National quotas in this capital fund should be based on the national incomes of the member countries and be payable in the currency of the subscribing country. Twenty per cent of each country's quota should be payable on joining ICCH for the general fund of ICCH (referred to as the "free" capital or "revolving fund" of ICCH). The remainder of a country's subscription would be callable by the board cn consent of the country concerned and earmarked, when subscribed, for the purchase of surplus commodities in that country. The ICCH should be empowered to accept subscriptions in convertible currencies from any country, in addition to its authorized quota, for the purchase of surpluses of the contributing country. All receipts and outgoings from transactions arising from original earmarked capital or added contributions, as distinct from "free" capital, should be held in a special account for the contributing country. Replenishment of capital, when needed, would be dependent upon additional subscriptions of capital by member countries burdened with surpluses.
Further down that page we have two other paragraphs which, taken with the one I just read, I think will give anyone a fairly good picture of the objective in view and the means by which it is proposed' to attain that objective:
(1)	The exporting country would sell surplus wheat to ICCH at full market price and the purchase would be financed by the exporter contributing the value of the wheat to ICCH as additional capital. ICCH would then sell quantities of wheat to the importing country in addition to and not as a substitution for its usual purchases. ICCH would take in payment the currency of the importing country, even if it were at the time inconvertible. The importing country would guarantee against loss by currency devaluation. ICCH would hold this currency to the credit of the exporting country until enlarged trade or restored currency convertibility permitted clearing the account.
(2)	The exporter would sell surplus wheat to ICCH at a reduced price if the payment were in an immediately acceptable (presumably convertible) currency and provided that the quantity of wheat went to some special use in addition to regular consumption by the importing country. Such transactions would be financed from the revolving fund of ICCH established by the initially paid-in 20 per cent of capital, but would not normally involve any loss to ICCH.
I imagine practically everyone realizes, as I am sure the Minister of Agriculture must realize, that this proposal would be far too costly for the nations to participate in if the money required to finance it had to be taken from the people of those countries by means of taxation or by adding to their national debts. But if a contributing country were able to create debt-free money against the surpluses within its borders and make a contribution of that created money, the situation would be very different. It has been

suggested-and perhaps this is the suggestion the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) has in mind, which he is keeping such a secret-that an ordinary nation like Canada, in order to finance the sale of its surpluses in soft currency countries, or countries lacking United States or Canadian dollars, would raise the money itself to pay for the goods it was going to sell abroad on credit, and would itself buy the goods and send them abroad, thereby eliminating the need to use the international organization. I do not think I would have any objection to that, except this; that if the nation had to raise the money through taxation of its people to provide a fund with which to buy surpluses of goods in order to give them away, which is practically what it amounts to, that nation would soon find the burden utterly insupportable, and would resort to a limiting of production rather than go to the expense of buying its surpluses and sending them abroad.
This brings us to the feasibility or otherwise of the creation of debt-free money. I do not propose to enter upon a discussion of that matter this evening. I have discussed it already in considerable detail in speeches in this house on March 16 and February 21 of this year, and October 25 of last year. I believe the arguments I advanced on those occasions would justify anyone in giving pretty careful thought to the feasibility of the proposal to create debt-free money within a nation to the extent of the surplus goods to be found available for sale. I submit once more that unless this government and the government of the United States resort to some such device they are going to find their agricultural problem completely bewildering, as the United States is finding its agricultural problem today. Already in the United States there has been talk about the dumping of their products upon the markets of the world at low prices. If any action is taken along that line it will more and more destroy our chances of selling our goods, and will generally demoralize the markets of the world.
This indicates the sort of problems which confront us. We simply cannot solve those problems by laughing at any new ideas that come along. In the five years mentioned by the minister-yes, in the last fifty years- we have pretty well proved that the problem cannot be solved by any methods followed by the government so far. If Canada would create debt-free money, which it would be possible for her to create against the surpluses she could easily have, then we would be able to accept sterling in payment for our goods sold to Britain. Or we would be able to accept any other soft currency, with which we could shop around and obtain many of
27, 1950
Agricultural Prices Support Act the things we need. We would be able to store our surpluses and have something on hand in case of trouble. We would be able to finance barter arrangements, such as apparently were envisaged by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) the other day in that forward-looking speech of his.
The only limiting factor would be our productive capacity, together with our ability to become self-sufficient. Just being able to produce one or two commodities would not be enough. We should have to become more and more self-sufficient so our money would have a sound base, and then we would have no difficulty in creating debt-free money and putting it into circulation. Granted those two considerations, sufficient production from our abundant resources and a sufficient variety of production, we could do a great many things with debt-free money which to the orthodox financial mind appear utter impossibilities. Then we would be able to make ours a really expanding economy, rather than the restricted economy it is rapidly becoming.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word on this measure in view of some of the statements made in the debate thus far. Then I listened to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) this afternoon suggesting, if I understood him correctly, that we should concentrate on the United States market rather than the United Kingdom market. Certainly I am one of those who have always been in favour of the United States market, but the sad position is that the farmers of the United States invariably have the very same type of surpluses we have, and that makes things rather difficult.
Every year since I have been here I have stated that never since confederation have the farmers of this country received their proper share of the national income. They have never done so up to date. If my memory serves me correctly, according to the figures put out by this government, during the first world war the agriculturists of Canada received approximately 29 per cent of the national income. During the recent world war they received approximately 18 per cent of the national income.
We have been discussing markets of recent years, and current markets. According to the Sanford Evans statistical bureau, which is

Agricultural Prices Support Act very reliable, a detailed survey for the first full calendar year following the war, 1946, reveals that our farmers in Canada suffered a loss of $378 million, over and above the great loss they had taken in the marketing of wheat. This is for livestock and coarse grains alone. This is a gigantic sum. When you have listened to the discussion today on the matter of tariffs and what not, when you take this amount of $378 million over and above the hundreds of millions of dollars lost in the marketing of wheat, it makes the great losses our western farmers have suffered because of tariffs look like peanuts.
In considering the matter of a formula, I have always advocated, since this act was brought into being, some formula based to some extent on parity; that is, a basis related to what it costs a farmer to produce these commodities. I believe that is a reasonable request. The farmer has not been receiving that. I have given you the figures for the full year of 1946, in which the farmer lost that great amount of money in comparison with what his neighbours in the United States received for marketing the same quantity of commodities. I believe we should bear that in mind. As I say, I followed the member for Provencher, but if I understood his argument it was not in agreement with a pamphlet put out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). It is entitled "Foreign Trade" and is dated December 10, 1949. It states:
During recent years, as much as 44 per cent of our farm production has entered export trade. To take wheat again, as an example, about 75 per cent of our production has been sold abroad.
I realize that although some hon. members made their entire speech on wheat, it does not come under this act. Other farm production, however, is tied to the price of wheat; you cannot get away from that. These are rather startling figures. If we lose that export trade, then our farm people will not enjoy prosperity. I have never known a time in any nation, when agriculture was not prosperous, that anyone else in that nation was prosperous. I do not think you can get away from that. It is very important.
I was pointing out that it is quite important that the farm producer should receive prices which will compensate him for the cost of production. I have an interesting article before me, an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on March 20. It is entitled "It's Cheaper in Minneapolis." It reads as follows:
Here in Winnipeg comparable cars cost approximately 20 per cent more than in Minneapolis. Refrigerator, range, vacuum cleaners, radio, and washing machine cost is 30 per cent more. In part this is traceable to the depreciated value of the


Canadian dollar-90 cents in terms of U.S. currency -in great part however, it is due to the Canadian tariff and various Canadian taxes.
The article goes on to point out:
It is also possible because in all cases the articles chosen for comparison were articles produced by the same companies either in the United States or in branch plants in this country. All must pay the 10 per cent premium either for the whole article or for the imported components which go into the Canadian-produced goods.
To this there is one exception-electric ranges, the standards for which differ in Canada and the United States but do not materially affect costs.
The article points out that these two central points, Minneapolis and Winnipeg, are in the centre of the two nations, about the same distance from the great manufacturing centres. In the case of a Ford automobile-I suppose some people think our farmers are not entitled to an automobile-the price in Winnipeg is $2,037, and in Minneapolis it is $1,597. There is a like comparison in trucks, which are essential on farms today. In automotive parts, an eight-cylinder assembly for a Ford costs $255 in Winnipeg, and $231 in Minneapolis. An RCA Victor eight-tube radio phonograph costs $289 in Winnipeg, and $150 in Minneapolis. A certain type of electric range costs $369 in Winnipeg, and $244 in Minneapolis. There are many other articles listed on which similar comparisons are made.
On the following day, March 21, another article appeared on the editorial page of the Winnipeg Free Press comparing these prices. It is entitled "You pay more in Winnipeg." This article deals with electrical goods. It points out that electric clocks cost 40 per cent more in Canada than the same articles in Minneapolis. Glassware, clothing and other articles are also compared. It points out that the tariff is somewhat responsible for this condition of affairs. I do not believe there was ever a time since confederation when certain of these industries had greater protection than they have today, in these controls, taxes and embargoes applied by this government. All this adds to the cost of the agricultural producer of this country, and to the cost of living of every consumer of this country. There is no argument whatever about that. During a debate the other day, I placed on Hansard a set of figures which had to do with agricultural products in their raw state, and a comparison of the prices at St. Paul, Winnipeg and Minneapolis of the manufactured article. In the majority of cases the prices for the raw materials were considerably higher in Minneapolis than in Winnipeg, but when one came to purchase the processed article the prices were reversed, and were higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis. In many cases the cost of living in Minneapolis

is cheaper than in Winnipeg. I believe that is proof that there is something radically wrong with our set-up in this country.
I am not unmindful of the fact that, I believe it was two years ago, a cost of living inquiry was conducted. It cost the taxpayers of this country a large sum of money, and proved nothing. Many members of this house spent a lot of time on that committee, but the outcome was a farce. Nothing was proven, despite the great cost of that committee. I just wanted to point out how unfairly the farmer has been treated by the government of the day. I have given the house a set of figures covering the cost of articles, which I think are essential on any farm, and which affect the consumers of this country as well. Neither the farm producer nor the Canadian consumer has been fairly dealt with by this government up to date. I think it is essential that we pass this type1 of legislation.
The ex-prime minister, in statements in 1943 and in the years following that, and the Minister of Agriculture as well, have made statements that, in view of the fact the agricultural producer in Canada was not receiving for his commodities prices comparable to those received in other countries, this situation should be taken into account in the years following the war. It is true that some articles bring fair prices today. I do think it is essential that a formula of some nature be written into this act, whereby the farm producer would have some idea, before the production period, of the basis upon which he would be paid during that production year. I believe that is very important. It is not only important to the farm producer, but it is also important to the consumer of this country.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to take only a few moments this evening mainly to speak about the problem which confronts our fruit growers in British Columbia. I shall be brief because the matter was covered fully and completely by the hon. members for Yale (Mr. Jones) and Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I should like to associate myself with what they said in that connection, and to add my voice to those which have been addressed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in requesting that some action be taken now, and that an announcement be made now, as to the assistance to be given to the British Columbia fruit growers, in view of the difficulties they face in marketing the 1949 crop.	.
There is a good deal of controversy around this question of support prices and support price legislation. It is not my intention to enter fully tonight into that controversy, although I support the principle that some assurance should be given to our farmers that they will have steady prices, that some measure should be provided by which they will be guaranteed their full share of the national income.
Whatever may be the views and controversy with regard to floor prices, it seems to me that there should not be any room for controversy with regard to the extending of assistance this year to the British Columbia apple growers. They are facing an emergency which is not of their own making and against which they are powerless to act, an emergency arising from the loss of their markets. I sometimes think that the permanent solution to the difficulties of constant or recurring surpluses and depressed prices followed by years of shortages and rising prices should not be sought merely in subsidies or a floor prices program, but should be combined with the building up of the domestic market so that we are better able to consume at home some of the things that we produce.
I do not suggest that we could ever make ourselves entirely self-sufficient, but I do think that we should aim constantly at producing in Canada a more balanced economy so that we are not so vulnerable and completely exposed, as we are now to the loss of overseas export markets. I am convinced that no solution will be complete unless and until steps are taken which will build and maintain a domestic market of really large proportions.
I should like to read one section of the Agricultural Prices Support Act which the bill now before us seeks to extend for another year. Section 9, subsection 2 reads:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable


returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION IN FORCE ON AND AFTER MARCH 31, 1950
speechtext: I should like to correct one statement which the hon. member made. The hon. member suggests that the act is to be extended for just one year whereas the bill provides that the act shall continue in force on and after March 31, 1950.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION IN FORCE ON AND AFTER MARCH 31, 1950
speechtext:
That was an inadvertent error; the time limit is being removed by the amendment. It seems to me that that section which I just read is the section to which we should be directing our attention, the necessity of ensuring to our farmers a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations. I do not think we can do that by prices support legislation alone because we will be faced, as the fruit growers now are faced, with vanishing markets and then where would we get the revenue to pay the support prices? That would not be available without increasing our population and building up a home market less vulnerable to the adverse conditions which now face our overseas markets. I think the two measures must go hand in hand and I urge the government to round out their prices support program by taking steps to build up our domestic market.
I turn more particularly to the problem faced by our fruit growers. Hon. members have heard of this before and I need not rehearse it in full. Their whole production and marketing program was geared largely to the existence.of a market in the United Kingdom which through no fault of their own has now virtually vanished. As has been said before, a fruit grower's program is a matter of twelve to fifteen years. It takes that long to get a tree into full bearing. It is something that cannot be changed overnight. Surely the answer is not to go around pulling out more fruit trees and cutting down production. It seems to me that under those circumstances the fruit growers are entitled to the assistance of support prices, during those years when their markets have vanished, in order to tide them over their difficulties.
I should like to refer to the rising costs with which they are also faced. When you go into a store to buy an apple, particularly one of those wonderful British Columbia apples, you sometimes do not realize the high quality of the product you are getting. Sometimes Ontario members seem to be surprised when they are told what has gone into getting that apple to the market. First there is the planting of the trees, the tending of the trees each year, the spraying, pruning, irrigating, thinning; then there is the buying

of the boxes, the packing of the boxes, hauling the boxes to the packing house, grading the apples, stamping the boxes and loading on the railroad cars. All those factors enter into the cost of production and marketing and every single item has increased during the last five years. Our growers are faced with tremendously increased costs and virtually disappearing markets.
As the house knows, the British Columbia growers were faced with a surplus this year that appeared to be unmarketable. Not wanting to see it go to waste and knowing that there was a shortage of this type of food in the United Kingdom they decided to make a gift of one million boxes of apples. The indications are that had they not sent that million boxes to the United Kingdom they would have been faced with a surplus of a million boxes or more for which no market could be found.
In view of what has been said during this debate and on other occasions, I hope the minister will no longer take the position that the British market is not a potential market for Canadian apples. The figures of apples purchased from other soft currency countries and even from the United States completely disprove the contention that the British are now producing their full domestic requirements in apples. I hope the minister will not continue to take the position that the United Kingdom is not an attractive market for us.
I hope he will give careful consideration to the suggestion put forward Thursday by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that in negotiating food contracts with the United Kingdom in the future he will use every endeavour to persuade them to take $4 million or $5 million out of their allocation to buy apples in Canada instead of concentrating their spending upon wheat and one or two other things on which they now spend relatively large sums.
I ask the minister if he will let us know before this debate is concluded whether he will accede to that request. Will he let us know particularly what assistance will be given to our apple growers this year and when they may expect to receive it?

I believe the time has
come when this prices support legislation should be made permanent, and we are pleased to see that is what the minister is endeavouring to do now. The farmers of Canada are in need of such security. They are not begging for it, by any means. It should be realized now that this is something they were promised during the war years. We all recall that during those years, when the prices of agricultural products were restricted and controlled and the farmers were forced to take less than they could get in the open market, they were assured that they would not lcse in the long run by having their prices controlled. This is one way the government is taking to see that those promises are kept, at least partly; and for that I think the government should be commended. But of course it depends entirely upon what the floor price is going to be.
At this point may I urge that the floor price should not be below parity price for those things the farmers have to buy. In my judgment it is a shame that some supporters of the government, and more than that some who are in very responsible positions, should be permitted to go about the country making irresponsible statements. Some of the parliamentary assistants have been travelling about the country saying things which are not to the
Agricultural Prices Support Act credit of either the party to which they belong: or themselves. If those statements are not correct it is time the cabinet ministers, who are responsible for carrying out the policies of this government, corrected them; and it is also time they put these parliamentary assistants in their place. I want to refer to some of those statements for a moment, and I am going to quote from the Manitoba Co-Operator of February 23. The heading is "Hannam says Canadian farmers seeking reasonable price levels," and the dispatch goes on:
Strong exception was taken by H. H. Hannam, president, Canadian federation of agriculture, to the remarks made by Leslie Mutch, M.P., parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, in an, address on Wednesday to the Liberal businessmen's club in Toronto.
Why the assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs should be taking over the Department of Agriculture as well is quite beyond my comprehension; but apparently be is straightening out that department at the-same time.

Mr. Mutch was quoted as saying that the almost universal demand for some sort of security was evidence of a softening of the moral fibre, a narcotic of the weak-willed, excuse of the lazy and the refuge of the coward.

The article goes on:
In a statement issued at Ottawa, Mr. Hannam said:
"If Mr. Mutch's remarks are to be taken seriously, they exhibit a most unfortunate attitude of mind...
He might have said "state of mind."
. . . and it is sincerely to be hoped he does not reflect the opinion of his minister or his government."
I think it high time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made a statement in that connection, so we may see whether or not the parliamentary assistant was expressing the opinion of his department or of the government, because after all one must remember that he occupies a responsible position.
"His remarks envision a return to the old economic anarchy of the past, wherein every man was for himself and the devil take the hindmost."
Now I would ask the parliamentary assistant who made that statement why, if there is any element of truth in what he said, the farmers are a fear-ridden bunch, or a lazy class of individuals. If there were any truth it would be because of the policies of this government. One has only to refer back to the hungry thirties to recall that one of -the most poverty stricken groups in Canada were the farmers, who continually sold their goods for less than the cost of production. No other industrial group in Canada has ever been asked to do that. A short time ago mention was made of these other industrial groups that have protection, and at that time something was said about tariffs. These are a very definite protection for those producing secondary goods. Take the machines the farmer has to buy. The Massey-Harris Company is one of the greatest producers of farm equipment in the world, I would say, with markets all over the world; yet farm machinery is protected by a tariff. Take the manufacturers who make automobiles and trucks. No industrial group in Canada has greater protection; yet those are the very implements the farmer has to buy. So when the farmers ask for a little protection in this prices support act they are not asking for charity. They are only asking for the same thing that other organizations have had ever since Canada was created, and something they were promised because of the low prices they took during the war.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION IN FORCE ON AND AFTER MARCH 31, 1950
speechtext: Why not pass the bill and let them get it?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION IN FORCE ON AND AFTER MARCH 31, 1950
speechtext:
I am not so sure they will; that is the thing I am fearful of, that by the time this is put into operation the floor prices will be so low the farmers will not be getting anywhere near parity prices. May I say right here that I am of the opinion that


the prices should be included in the bill, so
the farmers would know exactly what they were going to get. The prices should be based on parity.
When we think of the trend in agricultural prices, it is not much wonder that the farmers across the country are fearful. Let me quote from another clipping which I took from the Manitoba Co-operator of March 23, 1950. It is headed, "Farm living costs advance but total farm costs lower." It reads as follows:
Over-all costs of commodities and services used by Canadian farmers showed a slight drop in the five months from August last year to January this year, while farm living costs increased, according to indexes compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Farther down the article continues:
Reflecting increases for foods, fuel, health and maintenance, and miscellaneous items for both eastern and western Canada, the index of farm family living costs rose from 174-5 for August to 175-3 for January. The latest index was 3-5 points above the index for January, 1949. Clothing and household-equipment remained unchanged in the five months.
Indexes for farm equipment and materials increased 4-2 points, rising from 180-2 to 184-4, the latter level comparing with 180-3 in January last year. Among its components, price indexes were higher in January this year than in August for farm machinery, building materials, gasoline, oil and grease, feed, fertilizer, seed and hardware, but was unchanged for binder twine, while all sub-groups moved higher than a year ago except seed.
Is it any wonder then, Mr. Speaker, that the agriculturists are fearful lest the prices which are set under this bill are not going to be sufficient to give them anywhere near parity, when you realize that the figures I have just read indicate that the prices of those things which the farmers buy, and which are necessary to their production are all increasing? Is it any wonder that the farmers are fearful lest the prices which are set under this bill will not be sufficient to give them a fair return? I do not want to talk the bill out, or to carry it past eleven o'clock, but I do want to say that I think the minister would be doing justice to himself and the department if he were to put in this bill a price formula which would be parity for the farmers.

speechtext:
I am afraid it is rather late to start taking a vote on this bill tonight. We would have hesitated to move an amendment to this bill had it not been for certain statements which the minister made on Thursday during the resolution stage of this bill. It had been hoped that when this act was to be continued indefinitely the government would be prepared to set floor prices under the act which would be reasonably satisfactory to the agriculturists of this country. But when the minister was giving his explanation, that did not appear to be

what the government were going to do. He stated that they were using certain years, 1943, 1944, and 1945, to determine what the relationships were during those years, between what the farmer was receiving for what he had to sell and what his costs were.
Then he went on to say that did not necessarily mean that, although they used those years to get those relationships, the government was prepared to maintain that relationship. In fact, he said the opposite.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION IN FORCE ON AND AFTER MARCH 31, 1950
speechtext: What I really did say was that there was not any place where they did undertake to give the exact relationship. I went on to say that the United States makes it 60 per cent in one case, 90 per cent in another, and so on.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION IN FORCE ON AND AFTER MARCH 31, 1950
speechtext:
So that we can be sure of what the minister said, may I quote from page 1076 of Hansard:
The period we have been checking on is 1943, 1944 and 1945. We will continue to check on it. I do not say, neither do they in the United States, that when that has been worked out we are going to pay a 100 per cent floor price based on it. In the United States, they do not pay anything higher than 90 per cent, and most of the time they are paying 60 per cent.
I think the minister is wrong about that, because* the United States is paying 90 per cent on most of the basic products, not 60 per cent. On some of the perishable products, 60 per cent is being paid, but on the nonperishable products they are paying 90 per cent.
The minister continues as follows:
What I did say in Niagara Falls, and what I have said everywhere, is that, when we brought in this legislation, no farmer in Canada, no one anywhere, expected that we would set floor prices at the highest price level we would ever obtain from farm products.
We are not asking him to set them at the highest price level. We are asking him to
